Auditor/design reference. The consumer-facing purpose, API sketch, and verify
steps live in `README.md`; this document is the decision-process pipeline, the
two-way reachability rule (with the ISO cite), the metric handling, the next-hop
resolution, the intern mapping, and the list of what is not done.

**Where we are ahead:** exact directed-metric handling with the ISO Annex C.2.4 clause quoted and frozen against live FRR (asymmetric links resolve to the same cost as FRR), a deterministic sorted-intern so identical databases give byte-identical tables, and `asymmetric_links`/`reject_asymmetric` reporting that is SPB-relevant (802.1aq needs symmetric metrics); bounded, allocation-free next-hop resolution. **Where we are behind:** LAN transit is folded into member-to-member arcs (distances exact, but no pseudonode vertex in the tree); prefix routes cover the wide-metric TLVs #135/#236 only (no legacy #128/#130 narrow forms, no MT, no SR/Flex-Algo attributes); no incremental SPF (measured, see *What is deliberately not done*). Overload-bit transit exclusion (§3.6), ECMP next-hop sets (§3.7), IP/IPv6 prefix routes (§3.8), the attached-bit default (§3.9) and L1/L2 leaking (§3.10) are built.

## 1. Scope

The IS-IS **decision process** (ISO/IEC 10589 §7.2) for ONE level: read a
synchronised link-state database (`isis-lsdb`) and produce a forwarding table
`dest system-id → { next-hop system-id, total metric }`. Pure and deterministic;
no I/O, no clock (time is only forwarded to `isis-lsdb` so lifetimes age to the
caller's `now`). Point-to-point links and LAN segments (via the LSP of the pseudonode,
§3.2b) are routed; IP prefixes, ECMP, overload and the attached default are opt-in or default-on options of `Options`; out of scope: *What is deliberately not done*.

## 2. What each dependency provides

- **`isis`** (codec) — `Lsp.decode` exposing `lsp_id [8]`, `tlv_bytes`, and
  `tlvIterator()`; the reachability TLV views `ExtIsReachIterator` /
  `ExtIsReachEntry` (#22: 7-octet `neighbour_id`, `u24 metric`) and
  `IsReachIterator` / `IsReachEntry` (#2: `default_metric u8` + 7-octet
  `neighbour_id`). All bounds-checked: a lying length is a typed error, never an
  over-read.
- **`isis-lsdb`** (store) — `iterator(now) → ViewIterator` yielding `EntryView`
  with `lsp_id`, owned PDU `bytes`, and `is_request`. This module only reads it.
- **`spf-ect`** (graph) — the `Graph` builder (`ensureNode`, `addArc`
  (**directed**, one weight per direction) / `addEdge` (both directions at one
  weight), `Weight = u32 ≥ 1`, `Distance = u64`), `shortestPathTree(gpa,
  graph, root) → Tree` (Dijkstra + the ECT tie-break already applied), and
  `Tree.pred` / `distanceTo` / `reachable`.

This module owns: topology extraction, the two-way check, the system-id ↔ NodeId
intern, graph construction, and next-hop/metric resolution.

## 3. The pipeline

### 3.1 Topology extraction

Iterate the LSDB at `now`. Skip request placeholders (no bytes), and every LSP whose Remaining Lifetime
has aged to zero at `now` or that is a purge (ISO/IEC 10589 §7.3.17; `isis-lsdb` reports the aged
lifetime, so a caller that has not ticked its database still gets expired LSPs excluded). Decode each LSP
(a decode failure skips only that LSP). A **pseudonode LSP** (LSP-ID octet 6 ≠ 0)
contributes only the set of ISs it lists (§3.2b); it is never an origin. The
origin of every other LSP is `lsp_id[0..6]`. Walk the LSP's TLVs; from #22 and
#2 records collect directed advertisements `(from ⟶ neighbour[0..6], metric)`. A
**pseudonode neighbour** (neighbour-id octet 6 ≠ 0) is recorded as the member's
advertisement toward that 7-octet pseudonode id instead. A #22 advertisement at RFC 5305 §3's max-link-metric (`max_link_metric`, 0xFFFFFF) is excluded outright, not
added as a very expensive edge, so it cannot become the path of last resort. A malformed TLV or reachability record terminates that LSP's walk
(the records parsed before it still count); every other LSP is unaffected.

Directed advertisements are deduped per ordered `(from, to)` pair, keeping the
**minimum** metric (a link advertised via both #2 and #22, or across LSP
fragments, resolves to its best cost).

### 3.2 Two-way connectivity check (ISO/IEC 10589 §7.2.8.2)

Verbatim, from the clause (§7.2.8.2 "Two-way connectivity check"):

> "The Decision Process shall not utilise a link between two Intermediate
> Systems unless both ISs report the link.
> NOTE – the check is not applicable to links to an End System.
> Reporting the link indicates that it has a defined value for at least the
> default routeing metric. **It is permissible for two endpoints to report
> different defined values of the same metric for the same link. In this case,
> routes may be asymmetric.**"

The link {A, B} is admitted **only if both A⟶B and B⟶A were advertised**, and
each direction then enters SPF as its own arc at its own metric — the clause
decides whether a link is *used*, never what it *costs* (§3.3). The check
prevents a stale one-directional LSP — a neighbour that has gone away but whose
LSP has not yet aged out, or a half-formed adjacency — from creating a
forwarding path that does not exist.

The check has **no public off switch**: `Options` has no `require_two_way` field (a test asserts its
absence), so no production caller can disable it by accident. The **positive control** is a private,
test-only entry point (`computeWithBrokenTwoWayForTesting`) that admits a single directed
advertisement, mirroring it onto the direction nobody reported. It is deliberately wrong and exists
only so a permanent test can show that disabling the check makes the one-way link appear — i.e. that
the two-way check is the load-bearing part, not an accident of the topology.

### 3.2b LAN transit through pseudonodes

ISO 10589 Annex C / RFC 1195 model a LAN as a pseudonode vertex: member X
reaches it at X's own advertised metric, and it reaches every member at cost 0.
`addLanArcs` folds the zero-cost half in: for every pair of **admitted** members
X ≠ Y of pseudonode P it adds the arc X ⟶ Y at metric(X ⟶ P). That gives the
same distances as a pseudonode vertex, without a zero-weight arc (which
`spf-ect` rejects) and without a vertex that could appear as a destination or
next hop. A member is admitted when the two-way check passes on the LAN: X
lists P, and P's LSP (any fragment) lists X — the pseudonode speaks for the
LAN, as each router speaks for its P2P links. Where a P2P arc X ⟶ Y exists as
well, the cheaper one wins. The broken positive control (see 3.2) admits a member that lists P without P's confirmation. Metrics toward a
pseudonode are clamped to ≥ 1 like every other arc.

### 3.3 Metric handling: one arc per direction

IS-IS metrics are per-interface, so the two ends of a link may advertise
different costs, and the SPF is directed. ISO/IEC 10589 Annex C.2.4 ("The
Algorithm"), Step 1, verbatim:

> "compute
>   dist(P,N) = d(P) + metric_k(P,N).
> for each neighbour N (both Intermediate System and End system) of the system
> P. … d(P) is the second element of the triple ⟨P,d(P),{Adj(P)}⟩ and
> **metric_k(P,N) is the cost of the link from P to N as reported in P's Link
> State PDU**"

So the weight used to relax P→N is P's *own* advertisement for N, for the
direction actually being traversed. Each admitted direction therefore becomes
its own `spf-ect` arc (`Graph.addArc`) at its own metric; nothing is merged.
FRR 10.3 reaches r3 at cost **15 via r5**, and so does this module — the FRR
anchor test in `src/root.zig` asserts the agreement.

No single per-link weight could do this: which direction of a link a path traverses is decided by
the tree being computed, so the needed weight is not knowable when the graph is built.

Also:

- a metric of 0 is clamped to **1**: `spf-ect` rejects a zero weight because a
  0-cost arc can produce a predecessor 2-cycle that makes tree walks loop. A
  genuinely 0-cost IS-IS link is treated as cost 1.
- old-style #2 default metric: the **low 6 bits** of the octet are the value;
  the high bits are I/E / supported flags.

**Asymmetry is reported, not refused.** §7.2.8.2 permits it outright, so:

- `RouteTable.asymmetric_links` counts the admitted links whose two endpoints
  advertised **different** metrics. The routes are exact either way. It matters because IEEE 802.1aq *requires*
  symmetric metrics for congruent forward/reverse paths, so an SPB fabric with
  a non-zero count is misconfigured.
- `Options.reject_asymmetric` (**default `false`**) is the opt-in
  form of that check: `error.AsymmetricMetric` instead of a
  correct-but-asymmetric table. `compute` never uses it (its `Allocator.Error`
  signature is compiled against by `isis-sim` and `spbfib`).

### 3.4 Intern mapping (system-id ↔ NodeId)

The node set is every endpoint of an admitted edge, plus the local system-id if
it originated an LSP (so an isolated local system still yields a self route).
Note that every two-way edge endpoint is necessarily an LSP origin (to advertise
back, it must have originated an LSP), so a "dangling neighbour" — advertised but
with no LSP of its own — never advertises back, contributes no edge under the
two-way check, and is simply unreachable.

The system-ids are **sorted ascending** and assigned dense NodeIds `0..n` in that
order. This is deliberate, not incidental:

- **Determinism.** The LSDB is an `AutoHashMap`; its iteration order is not a
  stable contract. A "first-seen" NodeId assignment would leak that order into
  which equal-cost path the ECT tie-break selects. Sorting removes the
  dependency, so identical databases produce byte-identical tables.
- **Canonical tie-break.** `spf-ect`'s ECT tie-break prefers the "low path id".
  With NodeIds assigned in system-id order, that lines up with the standard
  lowest-system-id preference.

Because NodeIds ascend with system-id, iterating nodes `0..n` yields the route
table already sorted by destination.

### 3.5 Next-hop and metric resolution

`Tree.pred` is a parent-pointer chain (child → predecessor toward root). The
first hop toward a reachable destination `d ≠ root` is found by walking that
chain until the node whose predecessor **is** the root — allocation-free (no
`pathTo` slice is built). The total metric is `Tree.distanceTo(d)`. The local
node is `{ self, self, 0 }`; a direct neighbour resolves to itself.

### 3.6 Overload bit (ISO/IEC 10589 §7.2.8.1 / RFC 3787)

The overload bit of fragment 0 of a system's LSP (the other fragments' flags are
not read, ISO §9.8) marks it as not to be used for transit. After the arcs
are admitted, every arc *out of* an overloaded system other than the local one
is dropped (`Options.honour_overload`, default `true`): the system stays a
destination (the arcs into it remain, and so do the prefixes it advertises) but
no path runs through it. The local system's own bit is ignored in its own
computation. FRR, holo-isis and goisis honour it by default; `false` restores
the plain computation (SPB fabrics that never set it are unaffected). A pseudonode
LSP's flags are ignored. `isis-lsdb`'s generator sets the bit while the database is
overloaded (LSPDBOverload), which is what drains a system that ran out of room.

### 3.7 ECMP next-hop sets (`Options.max_paths`)

Default 1 (also 0): the single ECT-chosen path, as before. With `max_paths > 1` the
first hops of every shortest path are collected without `spf-ect` changes: an arc
`p ⟶ d` lies on a shortest path when `dist(p) + w == dist(d)`, and the first hops
of `d` are those of each such `p` (`d` itself when `p` is the root), processed in
ascending distance (weights are at least 1). The set is sorted by system-id, cut
to `max_paths`, listed by `RouteTable.nextHops` / `prefixNextHops`, and
`Route.next_hop` / `PrefixRoute.next_hop` is its lowest member. holo-isis has the same knob under
the name `max_paths`.

### 3.8 IP prefix routes (`Options.prefixes`, RFC 5305 §4, RFC 5308 §2)

Off by default (an SPB fabric has none). When on, the extraction also reads #135 and
#236 from every fragment of every non-pseudonode LSP (a malformed entry ends that TLV;
earlier entries count) into candidates. After the tree: each candidate whose
advertiser is reachable gets total metric `dist(advertiser) + advertised metric`
(`PrefixRoute.metric`, `u64`), and per prefix the best one is selected by, first
difference wins: a real advertisement before an attached-bit default (§3.9);
Up/Down clear before set (level 1; RFC 5302 §3.1 puts L1 intra-area before
L2->L1 inter-area, and §3.3 recommends ignoring the bit in L2 LSPs, so
`Options.level2` does); internal before external (the IPv6 X bit; RFC 5302 §3.1
ranks external routes below internal ones); the lower total metric; the lower advertiser
system-id. With `max_paths > 1` the candidates equal in all but the advertiser
(anycast) contribute all their first hops. The table is sorted by family, address,
length; `prefixRoute` / `prefixNextHops` look one up. Legacy narrow TLVs #128/#130
are not read (see below).

### 3.9 Attached-bit default route (`Options.attached_default`, needs `prefixes`)

ISO/IEC 10589 §7.2.9.2: a level-1-only system routes unknown destinations to the
nearest L1/L2 system that sets the attached bit. When the local LSP's IS Type is
not L1/L2, every reachable other system whose fragment 0 sets the default-metric
attached bit contributes `0.0.0.0/0` (if its #129 lists IPv4) and `::/0` (IPv6);
they are ranked below any advertised prefix, then by distance
(`PrefixRoute.attached_default`).

### 3.10 L1/L2 leaking (`leak.zig`, RFC 5302)

A L1/L2 system runs the computation once per level (the L2 one with `level2`) and
`leak.plan(gpa, l1_table, l2_table, policy)` turns the two tables into
`into_l2` / `into_l1` advertisement lists. L1 -> L2: every L1 prefix selected from
an advertisement with Up/Down clear, at the L1 total metric (RFC 5302 §3.1 default;
"Prefixes with the up/down bit set that are learned via L1 routing MUST NOT be
advertised by L1L2 routers back into L2"); attached defaults and
`Policy.l1_to_l2_deny` are excluded. L2 -> L1: only by policy
(`Policy.l2_to_l1`, covering prefixes), with Up/Down set and the L2 metric, and
not over a prefix the L1 computation holds natively. Metrics are clamped to
`MAX_PATH_METRIC`. `leak.addAdvert` builds the #135/#236 TLV for the generator
(`isis-lsdb`, `Origin.tlvs`). Whether a native L1 route blocks the leak is an
implementation choice (RFC 5302 gives the route preference, not this filter).

## 4. Degenerate cases (all documented, none panic)

| Case | Result |
|------|--------|
| Empty LSDB | empty table |
| Local has no LSP (not in the graph) | empty table |
| Local present but isolated | one row: the self route `{local, local, 0}` |
| Dangling neighbour (advertised, no LSP) | unreachable, absent from the table |
| Malformed reachability TLV | that record skipped; the rest still routes |

## 5. Memory / determinism

Everything allocated from the caller's `gpa` (directed map, pairs map, id set,
node↔id tables, graph, tree) is freed before returning; the leak check runs under
`std.testing.allocator`. The output `RouteTable` owns its `routes` slice, freed by
`deinit`. Given the same database and `now`, the table is byte-for-byte identical
across runs (a permanent test pins this).

## Verification

Run `scripts/modtest isis-spf`; the module's `example/main.zig` builds against the published module only.
Test classes (`src/root.zig` unless noted):

- **Golden topologies:** a line A-B-C with exact routes, next-hops and metrics; a 4-node path (the first hop to
  a distance-3 destination is the immediate neighbour); a diamond where the ECT tie-break picks a
  deterministic, stable next-hop; reconvergence after a failed link.
- **Two-way check:** a one-way advertisement yields no edge and adding the reverse creates it, with the
  positive control (the broken entry point DOES use the one-way edge); the absence of a public switch.
- **Extraction:** old-style #2 reachability and its default-metric mask (bits 7 and 6 of the octet, the I/E
  flag not folded into the value), the max-link-metric exclusion (and a normal alternate path still used),
  a metric of 0 clamped to 1 on a point-to-point link and on a LAN, the minimum of a pair advertised twice,
  a lifetime-zero LSP excluded.
- **LAN transit:** a 4-member LAN as a full mesh at each member's own metric, a LAN composing with a
  point-to-point tail, a member the pseudonode does not list back not admitted, a pseudonode listing nobody
  or one member, the pseudonode's own LSP never supplying a route, two LANs sharing a member not merging,
  a cheaper point-to-point arc beating a dearer LAN arc, both over #22 and over #2 TLVs.
- **Robustness and degenerate cases:** a malformed reachability TLV skipped with the rest still routing, a
  dangling neighbour unreachable, empty LSDB, local absent, local isolated; a leak check under
  `std.testing.allocator`; determinism (identical databases give byte-identical, sorted tables).
- **Asymmetric metrics:** each direction relaxes at its own metric, `asymmetric_links` counts and does not
  fire on a symmetric database, `reject_asymmetric` refuses.
- **FRR anchor:** a five-router topology (an asymmetric link, an equal-cost tie) computed once by a real
  `isisd` 10.3 and frozen into literal assertions; all five rows agree, and the old wrong shape is asserted
  not to come back (see Anchoring). The tests do not boot a VM or touch the network.
- **Fuzz:** two harnesses run by testkit's deterministic driver as `ISIS_SPF_FUZZ` (`src/fuzz_test.zig`):
  `isis-spf-compute` (hostile TLV regions spliced into stamped LSPs, both `compute` entry points) and
  `isis-spf-model` (random two-way graphs against a Floyd-Warshall model), each with a fixed seed loop and
  reach checks in every test run, and a corpus test that pins that the seeds reach the graph builder.
- **Constant time:** n/a, SPF over public data.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module
  mutation run and the delta runs after it.

## Open

- RFC 5305 §3 `MAX_PATH_METRIC` (0xFE000000), a ceiling on the SUMMED path cost, is not enforced. Nothing
  overflows (`Route.metric` is a `u64`); the difference is conformance: above the ceiling an RFC-conformant
  peer treats all path costs as equal, while this module keeps ordering them by their true sums, so an
  equal-cost tie-break could resolve differently at path metrics above 2^32. Closing it means clamping
  during relaxation, which lives in `spf-ect`; clamping only the reported metric would hide the difference.

## What is deliberately not done

- **Incremental / partial SPF.** Measured (`src/bench.zig`, `ISIS_SPF_BENCH`, ReleaseFast, 1000 systems in a
  ring with chords, four links each, 7 rounds of 20 calls): one full `compute` takes 2.7-3.1 ms
  (3.1-4.1 ms with prefixes), the bare shortest-path tree 0.60-0.78 ms, 21-27 % of it. Reusing the previous tree
  could save at most that share (1.3x at best, inside the spread of the numbers), the LSP walk and hash maps
  being the rest; skipping the walk needs a change log the LSDB does not keep. A recomputation of
  ~3 ms for 1000 systems is far inside any SPF hold-down timer. The rewrite is not shown to pay off and is
  not done.
- **Legacy narrow IP reachability (#128/#130) and wide/narrow metric styles.** Only RFC 5305/5308
  wide-metric prefixes are routed; the `isis` codec has no typed #128/#130 either.
- **Multi-topology SPF (RFC 5120).** One topology per computation (the SPB fabric and a plain IP area);
  MT TLVs #222/#235/#237 are not in the `isis` codec.
- **Pseudonode vertices** (LAN transit stays folded into member-to-member arcs, §3.2b).

## Backlog / deferred

None.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle MIXED

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle MIXED** — anchored for some paths, self for others — the evidence below names which.

**What the tests actually contain.** 5-router topology run once through real isisd 10.3 in-VM, matching vertex-by-vertex on all five rows with NO remaining gap (the "modulo documented undirected-engine gap" this line used to carry was superseded by the directed rewrite and is corrected 2026-09-03); rest stays SELF

The capture ran five real `isisd` instances, one per network namespace joined by veth with real IPv4 addressing
(load-bearing for the point-to-point three-way handshake), in the Debian VM lane (`scripts/vm/`); the `vtysh`
commands, FRR's version and the printed lines are quoted in the `FRR anchor` tests' shared comment. Nothing is
FRR source or FRR's own fixtures: a routing table computed for a topology authored here is output, not a work
based on the program (GPLv2 §0). What stays self-authored (SELF) is every other test above, LAN transit
included; multi-level leaking is out of scope.
